findings.title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public ServiceLoader SPI, but `order()` was added as an abstract method. Existing external implementations will no longer compile against this interface; implementations already compiled against the previous version can still be discovered but will fail with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` evaluates `CryptoProvider::order`. Provide a default order implementation (or otherwise version the SPI) so existing providers remain usable.

findings.title: Equal-priority FIPS and default providers are selected by unspecified ServiceLoader order
findings.body: DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200. When more than one is visible, this code now silently keeps whichever provider happens to appear first from ServiceLoader rather than failing as it did before. ServiceLoader ordering across jars/modules is not a safe configuration mechanism, so a FIPS deployment with both FIPS and default providers can select the non-FIPS provider. Moreover, all candidates are instantiated while collecting them, so the ignored FIPS provider can still mutate global Java security providers/properties. Reject equal highest-priority providers or make the selection explicit and ensure mutually exclusive providers cannot be silently ignored.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated default keystore provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract promises the BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the provider selected for the JVM's default keystore type (commonly `SUN` for JKS/PKCS12). That provider is unrelated to BouncyCastle and may not support algorithms callers expect from this method. Code using the CryptoProvider API can therefore receive a misleading provider and fail when it attempts BouncyCastle-specific operations. Return an actual registered BouncyCastle provider, or adjust the provider/API behavior so callers do not receive an unrelated provider.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests sign with a default P-256 key
findings.body: The test creates one `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` key pair without selecting a curve and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. The JDK default is typically P-256, so the ES384 and ES512 cases do not exercise 48- and 66-byte ECDSA coordinates/signatures that those algorithms require. Generate a key on the matching named curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature with the corresponding public key, rather than only checking a conversion round trip.
